title: Asian Refiners Turn to Argentina as War Reroutes Global Oil Flows; China LNG Imports Set to Drop 18% on Record Prices
subhead: The Iran war's supply shock is now reshaping trade routes far beyond Hormuz: Asian buyers are sourcing chokepoint-free crude from Argentina, Asia is filling Africa's diesel gap, and record LNG prices are starting to destroy Chinese demand. Europe gas hit its highest level since 2023 as US-Iran strikes resumed.

sections.heading: The War's Supply Shock Reroutes Global Trade Flows
sections.body:
Asian crude importers including China, Japan and South Korea have turned to buying oil from as far as Argentina to offset Middle East supply losses, anonymous traders told Bloomberg on Monday. Refiners have bought cargoes of Argentina's Medanito crude from the Vaca Muerta shale basin, which travels to Asia around South America and into the Pacific without crossing any chokepoint or canal. Argentina's oil sales to Asia have jumped this year from 2025, and from zero exports at all until 2024, per Argentinian government data compiled by Bloomberg.

The re-routing extends to refined fuels. Asia's diesel exports to Africa are surging to nearly five-year highs while Middle East sales to Africa crashed to nine-year lows, a Reuters analysis of ship-tracking data showed. Asian refiners are expected to have sent up to 15 million barrels of diesel to Africa in August, the most in at least four and a half years, as Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb threats plus the Houthi attack on Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery crippled Middle East supply. Jazan sent no diesel to Africa in August versus 163,000 tons in July, per Kpler data cited by Reuters.
sections.whyItMatters: The war is no longer just a chokepoint story — it is forcing a permanent-looking reconfiguration of global crude and fuel trade, with Argentina and Asia emerging as new suppliers of last resort.

sections.heading: Aramco Keeps Saudi Crude Flowing to China via Ship-to-Ship Handoffs
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco is offering more September crude to Asian buyers through ship-to-ship transfers outside Hormuz, according to Reuters, after shipping data showed Saudi barrels moving through the strait with tracking systems switched off. The model moves crude through the dangerous leg, then transfers it to another tanker off Fujairah in the UAE or Sohar in Oman. Aramco has opened sales of Arab Medium and Arab Heavy this way for a second consecutive week.

China is buying: two VLCCs carrying a combined 4 million barrels of Saudi crude were headed to China after receiving cargoes via ship-to-ship transfers off Sohar, per Vortexa and Kpler data cited by Reuters, with both cargoes destined for Sinopec. Aramco resumed loading at Ras Tanura and Juaymah earlier this month after a three-week pause, while routing more crude west through the East-West pipeline and Egypt's Sidi Kerir terminal for European customers.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia is absorbing the Hormuz risk itself to keep its largest customer supplied, a workaround that keeps barrels moving but signals the strait remains far from normal.

sections.heading: Europe Gas Hits Highest Level Since 2023 as US-Iran Strikes Resume
sections.body:
European benchmark natural gas prices jumped 5% in early Monday trade, with the Dutch TTF topping 70 euros ($81.20) per MWh — the highest front-month level in more than three and a half years, since January 2023, Oilprice.com reported. The re-escalation of US-Iran hostilities intensified concerns about LNG supply from the Middle East, on top of Qatar's extension of force majeure on LNG deliveries by one month through October.

Europe is heading into winter with one of the lowest gas storage levels in two decades, as the war crippled Qatari LNG supply and intensified Asia-Europe competition for cargoes that don't cross geopolitically charged chokepoints. Unlike crude, LNG cannot be shuttle-shipped through Hormuz and reloaded via ship-to-ship transfer, leaving LNG traffic at the strait at a standstill even as oil flows have rebounded.
sections.whyItMatters: With storage at a two-decade low and Qatari term deliveries absent, Europe enters winter structurally exposed to any further supply shock — and gas prices are already pricing that risk in.

sections.heading: Record LNG Prices Start Destroying Chinese Demand
sections.body:
China's LNG imports are on track to slump 18% in August from a year earlier, to about 5.2 million tons, bucking a three-month trend of growing purchases, per Kpler estimates cited by Bloomberg. The average spot LNG price for delivery into Asia nearly doubled year-on-year to $21 per MMBtu in August, versus $12 a year earlier, with spot prices hitting a five-month high of $23.388 per MMBtu last week.

Utilities in Asia have been outbidding Europe for LNG this summer amid a shrinking pool of Middle East cargoes that other producers cannot fully offset. The high prices are now leading to demand destruction among price-sensitive Chinese industrial consumers, ending a three-month run of higher imports.
sections.whyItMatters: The first clear sign of demand destruction in the world's largest LNG buyer — a signal that sustained high prices are now curbing consumption, not just reallocating it.

sections.heading: Chevron, ONGC and GE Vernova Near Final Venezuela Energy Deals
sections.body:
Chevron, India's ONGC, GE Vernova, Eni and GeoPark are preparing to sign final energy agreements in Venezuela, Reuters reported Monday, citing five sources. Venezuela has spent six months rewriting oil contracts under its amended hydrocarbons law, giving foreign companies more operational flexibility and allowing them to export their own crude and receive proceeds directly — a major departure from the state-controlled PDVSA model.

Chevron's agreements are expected to be 'of significant size,' seeking an additional Orinoco Belt block and an area in northern Monagas for diluents. ONGC is preparing to invest about $200 million in the San Cristobal field, targeting a tenfold production increase. The deals are separate from the larger US-Venezuela pact announced last week covering stakes in 17 oilfields with about 64 billion barrels of proved reserves.
sections.whyItMatters: Venezuela is moving from state control to a contract model that lets foreign firms capture export revenue directly — a structural shift that could meaningfully add non-Hormuz supply to a tight global market.

sections.heading: Critical Minerals and Nuclear Fuel Tighten: Lithium Profits, Uranium Surge
sections.body:
Lithium miners are reporting strong first-half profits on surging battery storage demand, Bloomberg reported. Chinese majors Tianqi Lithium and Ganfeng Lithium posted their biggest profits in three years, while US Albemarle said global lithium demand rose 45% year-on-year through May, driven largely by battery storage. The war in the Middle East has added a catalyst, as energy-importing countries double down on alternatives to reduce dependence on Middle East oil and gas.

Uranium prices are also gaining momentum, approaching $89 per pound in August after five months range-bound between $84 and $87, per Bloomberg futures data. A structural supply deficit, AI and data-center power demand, and China's nuclear buildout are tightening the market, with utilities accelerating procurement. China is expected to become the world's largest nuclear power market by the end of the decade.
sections.whyItMatters: The energy-security scramble is feeding directly into transition and nuclear supply chains — lithium and uranium are both tightening as importers hedge against fossil-fuel chokepoint risk.

sections.heading: Iran-Hormuz Update: Strikes Resume After Month-Long Lull
sections.body: US forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island inside the Strait of Hormuz after the IRGC were observed 'preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait,' per a US Central Command spokesperson, Oilprice.com reported. Iran retaliated by targeting two US air bases in Jordan, and Iran's Foreign Ministry said its armed forces 'will not hesitate to exercise the inherent right of self-defence.' Iran dismissed as 'laughable' a Trump Truth Social AI-generated post claiming Kharg Island was 'being blown to smithereens,' with NIOC chief Hamid Bovard saying conditions at Kharg — which handles about 90% of Iran's oil exports — are calm. Oil prices rose 3.6% in early European trade on the re-escalation.
sections.whyItMatters: The month-long lull is over, but the market's muted reaction — oil up only ~3.6% — suggests traders have largely priced in a conflict that keeps disrupting supply without fully closing the strait.

bottomLine: The Iran war's supply shock is now visibly reshaping global energy trade beyond the chokepoint itself: Asian refiners are sourcing chokepoint-free crude from Argentina, Asia is filling Africa's diesel gap, Saudi Arabia is absorbing Hormuz risk via ship-to-ship handoffs to keep China supplied, and record LNG prices are starting to destroy Chinese demand. Europe gas hit its highest level since 2023 with storage at a two-decade low, while Venezuela's shift to a contract model and tightening lithium and uranium markets point to a broader reallocation of supply and investment. The resumption of US-Iran strikes ended the month-long lull, but muted oil price reaction suggests markets have priced in a persistent, disruptive conflict rather than a full closure.
sources: Oilprice.com, Reuters, Bloomberg, Kpler, Vortexa, US Central Command, National Iranian Oil Company, Argentinian government data
